name: famous-buildings

description.en: 50 famous buildings and their architects: 39 of the world's best-known, ranked by their number of Wikipedia and other Wikimedia sitelinks in Wikidata, from Hagia Sophia and the White House to Fallingwater, and 11 Nordic buildings ranked the same way, from Drottningholm Palace to Stockholm City Hall (buildings of unknown, collective or disputed authorship left out). Front: the building, in English or Swedish, with its city where that helps; back: its architect or pair of architects, with a note on those who completed it. Taken from Wikidata and checked against the English and Swedish Wikipedia and official sites.
description.sv: 50 kända byggnader och deras arkitekter: 39 av världens mest kända, rangordnade efter hur många länkar till Wikipedia och andra Wikimediaprojekt de har i Wikidata, från Hagia Sofia och Vita huset till Fallingwater, och 11 nordiska byggnader rangordnade på samma sätt, från Drottningholms slott till Stockholms stadshus (byggnader med okänd, kollektiv eller omstridd upphovsman ingår inte). Framsida: byggnaden, på engelska eller svenska, med staden där det hjälper; baksida: arkitekten eller arkitektparet, med en anteckning om dem som fullbordade bygget. Uppgifterna är hämtade från Wikidata och kontrollerade mot engelska och svenska Wikipedia och officiella webbplatser.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

World ranking (query 1): as in the library's famous-sculptures deck, fame is measured by the number of Wikipedia (and other Wikimedia) sitelinks of a Wikidata item. Query 1 takes the items that are instances of building (Q41176) or of any subclass of it and have at least one architect (P84), the top 400 by sitelinks, with each item's architects and English and Swedish labels. It answered on query.wikidata.org on 2026-10-04 (680 rows, 400 items); the CSV was saved in the research scratch directory, which is not published.

Nordic ranking (query 2): the brief asks for Nordic buildings, and only Drottningholm Palace (59) and Helsinki Cathedral (51) appear in query 1's top 400 at all; neither reaches the world walk's 60-sitelink cut-off. A second ranking therefore takes the same items restricted to those whose country (P17) is Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland or Iceland, top 60 by sitelinks. It timed out on query.wikidata.org twice (HTTP 504, then a client time-out with the query optimiser switched off), so it was run on QLever's mirror of Wikidata (https://qlever.dev/api/wikidata), which the famous-sculptures deck also used. For the two buildings in both rankings the sitelink counts agree (Drottningholm Palace 59, Helsinki Cathedral 51).

Selection (see the selection): walking down query 1, a building became a card when the English Wikipedia (and, where it says so, the Swedish Wikipedia) names one architect, or a pair of architects jointly, as the designer of the building as it stands, and that attribution agrees with Wikidata's P84. The world walk stopped at 60 sitelinks (39 cards, from Hagia Sophia, 152, to Fallingwater, 60). The Nordic walk down query 2 applied the same rules and stopped at 38 sitelinks, which brings in Stockholm City Hall (38) as the brief asks: 11 cards, Drottningholm Palace (59) first. The excluded candidates and the reasons are listed in the selection. Quality-control round 1 removed two of the world cards first selected, the Sistine Chapel (attribution varies between the sources) and the Israel Museum (several architects, its main wings rebuilt in 2010), and named in the selection the candidates at or above 60 sitelinks that it had left out without naming them.

Data (query 3): fetch_all.py fetched the Wikidata entities of the 52 buildings first selected (two since removed, see round 1) and 26 excluded candidates and of all their architects (labels, aliases and claims in English, Swedish and mul; English and Swedish sitelinks), then the full plain text and revision id of each English and Swedish Wikipedia article linked from them. A second script (query 4) fetched the English articles on 32 further excluded candidates to document the exclusions. Summaries printed the sentences of each article that name an architect; every attribution was read in its context. In quality-control round 1 a further script (query 8) fetched the English articles on the further candidates then named in the selection, and the Portuguese and Italian articles on Mirante do Vale and the Sistine Chapel.

Back (the architect): Wikidata's P84 of each building. Where Wikidata lists more than one architect, the card names the architect or pair that the English Wikipedia names as the designer and a back note names those who completed or altered the building (Peter Hall at the Sydney Opera House, Tessin the Younger and Carl Hårleman at Drottningholm, Carl Hårleman at Stockholm Palace, Rondelet at the Panthéon, Parigi and Buontalenti at the Uffizi, Ludwig Hoffmann at the Pergamon Museum, Ernst Lohrmann at Helsinki Cathedral, Lauritz de Thurah at Amalienborg, Abadie's five successors at Sacré-Cœur). Wikidata's later or lesser architects are not named on the card: Trdat (repairs of 989) and Mimar Sinan at Hagia Sophia (Wikidata ranks Anthemius and Isidore as preferred), Heinrich Strack (later alterations) at the Brandenburg Gate, Sanquirico, Secchi and Mario Botta at La Scala (Piermarini is ranked preferred), Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and Fazlur Khan at the Willis Tower (Khan named in the note), Adamson Associates at the Petronas Towers, Maximilien Brébion at the Panthéon (Wikidata's third architect there, beside Soufflot and Rondelet; the English Wikipedia's account of the building does not name him). For the Palace of Westminster Wikidata's P84 names Charles Barry, Jr. (Q5075445), not his father Sir Charles Barry (Q552584), whom both Wikipedias name as the architect; the card follows the Wikipedias (see round 0).

Names: the English and Swedish names of the buildings are Wikidata's labels or aliases, which the builder checks against live Wikidata; Belvedere's Swedish front is its Swedish label "Schloss Belvedere" and the Gazprom Arena's Swedish front its Swedish alias "Gazprom Arena" (its Swedish label "Krestovskij stadion" is in the front note). The architects' names are their Wikidata English and Swedish labels or aliases, with five exceptions, four recorded in round 0 and one in round 5: the English "Bartolomeo Rastrelli" (the English Wikipedia's form; Wikidata's English label is "Francesco Bartolomeo Rastrelli"); the Swedish "Satyrus och Pythius" for the Mausoleum's architects (the Swedish Wikipedia's form; Wikidata has no Swedish label for Satyros and "Pytheos" for Pythius, and no Swedish text found uses "Pytheos", query 7); Mirante do Vale's two engineers, who have no Swedish labels and whose names Swedish writes unchanged; Leppänen of Petäjävesi, whose Wikidata labels are swapped (the English label is the Swedish form "Jacob Clementsson Leppänen", the Swedish label the Finnish form), so the card gives the English Wikipedia's "Jaakko Klemetinpoika Leppänen" in English and the Swedish Wikipedia's "Jacob Clementsson Leppänen" in Swedish; and the English "Sedefkar Mehmed Agha" for the Sultan Ahmed Mosque's architect (the English Wikipedia's spelling, which is also Wikidata's Swedish label; Wikidata's English label is the Turkish spelling "Sedefkar Mehmed Ağa").

Disambiguation: a front note gives the city (or, for the Gazprom Arena, its other name) where a name alone could mean another building or is little known: Barcelona, Chicago (with the former name Sears Tower), Istanbul, Dubai, Saint Petersburg, Milan, London, Florence, São Paulo, Amsterdam, Edirne, Paris, Cleveland, Berlin, Vienna, New York, Pennsylvania, Copenhagen, Malmö, Reykjavík and Stockholm. The British Museum's note says "the main building", since later parts are by others (the Round Reading Room by his brother Sydney Smirke), and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's that the card means the museum building. No note names or hints at the architect.

Cross-checks: every card's attribution was checked against the English Wikipedia (the sentence naming the architect is quoted verbatim from the full text of the revision read) and, for the 41 cards whose Swedish article names the architect, against the Swedish Wikipedia. Official pages were a further check where they could be read (query 5): the National Park Service (White House), Kungliga slotten (Drottningholm Palace, Stockholm Palace), Teatro alla Scala, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and Fallingwater (its "Designing Fallingwater" page). Mirante do Vale's designers were also checked in the Portuguese Wikipedia. Other official sites tried answered HTTP 404, timed out or carried no attribution in their text (the Rijksmuseum, Hallgrímskirkja, HSB (Turning Torso), the Sagrada Família, Nationalmuseum, the Centre Pompidou, the Pentagon tours site, the Sydney Opera House, the Guggenheim New York, The Shard and the Opéra de Paris); those cards rest on Wikidata and the two Wikipedias. Web searches (query 6) were used only to find official pages.

Notes: the notes are the compiler's own wording of facts; each fact has a quoted source in the card's evidence (the English or Swedish Wikipedia, or the official page). The Swedish notes and front notes were written directly in Swedish, with place names in their Swedish form (Florens, Wien, Köpenhamn, Sankt Petersburg, Milano).

Machine checks: for every card the builder checks against live Wikidata that the building's P84 includes the architect(s) on the card (for the Palace of Westminster, Augustus Pugin, named in the note, since P84 lacks Sir Charles Barry), the English and Swedish labels or aliases of the building that the front uses, and the English and Swedish labels or aliases of each architect the back names, except where round 0 records that the card's form is not in Wikidata. The builder accepts a multilingual (mul) label for any language. The deck was then validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (scripts/validate_sources.ts).

The dossier was assembled by a script (make_dossier.py, in the research scratch directory, which like the other helper scripts and the saved files is not published) from a hand-written card list: it checks that every quotation occurs verbatim in the saved article or page text (and stops if one does not), records the revision ids, writes the Wikidata evidence from the saved entities and generates the Wikidata label checks only where the card's text equals a Wikidata label or alias.
selection: About 50 famous buildings, chosen objectively in two passes. World: the Wikidata items that are buildings (instances of Q41176 or a subclass) with an architect (P84), ranked by their number of sitelinks (query 1, 2026-10-04), taken in rank order down to 60 sitelinks: 39 cards. Nordic: the same items in Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland or Iceland (query 2), down to 38 sitelinks: 11 cards. An item was left out when it is not a building or is an institution rather than a building (the Statue of Liberty, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, the Tretyakov Gallery, whose façade only is by Viktor Vasnetsov); when its maker is unknown, legendary or a hypothesis (the Great Pyramid of Giza and Hemiunu, Borobudur and Gunadharma, the Pantheon in Rome and Apollodorus, the Leaning Tower of Pisa, St Basil's Cathedral, whose architect the English Wikipedia calls unknown, the Taj Mahal, built by a board of architects, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, where Strabo records only Sostratus's dedication, Rosenborg Castle, with which two architects are only "associated", and the Charles Bridge, whose attribution to Peter Parler the English Wikipedia does not make); when the sources credit three or more architects, a firm or a team (the Louvre, St Peter's Basilica, Versailles, the Kremlin, the Forbidden City, the Capitol, Buckingham Palace, Windsor Castle, Neuschwanstein, the Metropolitan Museum and MoMA; the Israel Museum, where Alfred Mansfeld's buildings of 1965 stand beside Armand Bartos and Frederick Kiesler's Shrine of the Book and James Carpenter's pavilions, and whose main wings were completely rebuilt in 2010; the Van Gogh Museum, Gerrit Rietveld's building with Kisho Kurokawa's exhibition wing; the Musée d'Orsay, which the English and Swedish Wikipedia give to three architects, Lucien Magne, Émile Bénard and Victor Laloux, though Wikidata names Laloux alone; the Eiffel Tower, designed by Gustave Eiffel's company with the engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier and the architect Stephen Sauvestre; the Empire State Building (Shreve, Lamb & Harmon), Burj Khalifa (Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, where Wikidata lists five designers), One World Trade Center (Daniel Libeskind's plan replaced by David Childs's design), the CN Tower, the Stade de France, the Stadio Olimpico, Tokyo Skytree, the Mode Gakuen Cocoon Tower, the National Diet Library, Abeno Harukas, the Allianz Arena, Wembley, the Emirates Stadium, the Avicii Arena, the Oslo Opera House, the Ostankino Tower, the London Stadium and the FNB Stadium (Populous), the Lukoil Arena (AECOM), the Beijing National Stadium (Herzog & de Meuron), the Shanghai World Financial Center (Kohn Pedersen Fox), the Westfalenstadion, expanded several times, and other stadiums and towers credited to firms); when the medieval cathedral or palace was built over generations (Notre-Dame de Paris, Cologne, Milan, Chartres, Reims, Canterbury, Florence, St Vitus, St Mark's, Santiago de Compostela, Aachen, Saint-Denis, the Doge's Palace, Nidaros, Roskilde; likewise the Archbasilica of St. John Lateran, rebuilt over the centuries with Francesco Borromini's interior and Alessandro Galilei's façade, Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral, built in sections from 1573 to 1813, the Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba, a mosque of 785 expanded over two centuries with a Renaissance cathedral built into it, the Apostolic Palace, built mainly between 1471 and 1605, and 10 Downing Street, houses that William Kent joined and that were rebuilt many times since) or the person Wikidata names was its patron (Mehmed II at the Topkapı Palace, Abbot Suger, Absalon); when the attribution varies between the sources (the Sistine Chapel: the English and Swedish Wikipedia give it to Baccio Pontelli, but the Holy See's own page names Giovannino de' Dolci and Baccio Pontelli together; the Élysée Palace: the Swedish Wikipedia names Armand-Claude Mollet and Jean Cailleteau, the English Mollet; the Bolshoi Theatre: Joseph Bové from Andrei Mikhailov's design; Schönbrunn Palace, which the English Wikipedia gives to no architect; Big Ben, a bell whose tower Augustus Pugin designed within Charles Barry's palace, the Palace of Westminster having its own card; Balmoral Castle, William Smith's designs amended by Prince Albert; the Temple of Artemis, where Wikidata pairs Chersiphron with a later architect); when the building standing today is chiefly someone else's (the Reichstag, fundamentally redesigned by Norman Foster; the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, demolished in 1931 and rebuilt 1995–2000; the Quba Mosque, rebuilt in 1986; Tate Modern, Giles Gilbert Scott's power station converted by Herzog & de Meuron; the Hoover Dam, whose exterior only Gordon Kaufmann redesigned; Archibald Leitch's football grounds Old Trafford, Anfield, Stamford Bridge, Villa Park and Goodison Park, whose stands have been rebuilt, Everton having moved out of Goodison in 2025; Christiansborg Palace, now the third palace on the site, Häusser's being the first); and when it is being rebuilt as of 2026-10-04 (Camp Nou, under renovation since 2023). Facts are as of 2026-10-04; a building's architect does not change, though a building's name may (the Willis Tower and the Gazprom Arena carry their former or other name in the front note).
